questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Definite Integral of a Piecewise Linear Function Given Its Graph
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14032967/assets/22472e04f7bd26076da43a2ad17a192726ad19b5bd3885ce066c9523cad4f870.png)

The graph of $y=f(x),$ shown above, consists of three line segments. Find the value of ${\int }_{-2}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
The graph consists of three parts: the line segment for $x\in [-2,-1],$ the line segment for $x\in (-1,1),$ and the line segment for $x\in (1,3].$ Therefore, we can write the required integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-2}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-2}^{-1}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{-1}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={{{\int }_{-2}^{-1}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{-{A}_{1}}+{{{\int }_{-1}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{2}}+{{{\int }_{1}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

- The $1$st integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [-2,-1].$ The corresponding region is a right triangle. Therefore, we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}(bh) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(1\cdot 3) \\  & =1.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the region lies below the $x$-axis, we have

$$
{\int }_{-2}^{-1}f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{A}_{1}=-1.5.
$$

- The $2$nd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in (-1,1).$ The corresponding region is a trapezoid, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(a+b)h \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2+3)(2) \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

- The $3$rd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in (1,3].$ The corresponding region is a trapezoid, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{3} & =\frac{1}{2}(a+b)h \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(1+2)(2) \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-2}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x & =-{A}_{1}+{A}_{2}+{A}_{3} \\  & =-1.5+5+3 \\  & =6.5.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14032967/assets/3e0eca1a04396c0c86bbf5c3e5a9b3ff7071eacfe3d8c4281549e70cda809e8c.png)

Given the graph of $y=f(x)$ above, find the value of 
${\int }_{-2}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
The graph consists of $2$ parts: the line segment for $x\in [-2,3)$ and the arc of the quarter-circle for $x\in (3,5].$ So, we can use the additive property of integrals to get

$$
{\int }_{-2}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x={{{\int }_{-2}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{1}}+{{{\int }_{3}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{2}}.
$$

- The $1$st integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [-2,3).$ The corresponding region is a right triange, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot bh \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 5\cdot 2 \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

- The $2$nd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in (3,5].$ The corresponding region is a combination of an inverted quarter-circle of radius $2$ and a square, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & ={s}^{2}-\frac{1}{4}\pi {r}^{2} \\  & ={2}^{2}-\frac{1}{4}\pi (2)^{2} \\  & =4-\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-2}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={A}_{1}+{A}_{2} \\  & =5+(4-\pi ) \\  & =9-\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

If the graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown above, then

${\int }_{-4}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x=$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The graph consists of $2$ parts: the arc of the semi-circle for $x\in [-4,-2]$ and the line segment for $x\in (-2,1].$ So, we can use the additive property of integrals to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-4}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x={{{\int }_{-4}^{-2}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{1}}+{{{\int }_{-2}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

- The $1$st integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [-4,-2].$ The corresponding region is a semi-circle, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}\pi {r}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\pi \cdot (1)^{2} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- The $2$nd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in (-2,1].$ The corresponding region is a trapezoid, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(a+b)h \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2+1)\cdot 3 \\  & =\frac{9}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-4}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={A}_{1}+{A}_{2} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}+\frac{9}{2} \\  & =\frac{\pi +9}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14032967/assets/8eb7c4fe147028c6dc31aad2427a33bb713553e610101b1fd263bda30f5c49d0.png)

The graph $y=f(x),$ shown above, consists of three line segments. Then,

${\int }_{-6}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x=$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We divide the interval of integration into $4$ regions: the line segment for $x\in [-6,-4],$ the line segment for $x\in [-4,-3),$ the line segment for $x\in [-3,0),$ and the line segment for $x\in [0,5].$ Therefore, we can write the required integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-6}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x={{{\int }_{-6}^{-4}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{-{A}_{1}}+{{{\int }_{-4}^{-3}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{2}}+{{{\int }_{-3}^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{3}}+{{{\int }_{0}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{4}}.
$$

- The $1$st integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [-6,-4].$   The corresponding region is a triangle below the $x$-axis, so

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}(bh) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\cdot 2) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus,

$$
{\int }_{-6}^{-4}f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{A}_{1}=-2.
$$

- The $2$nd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [-4,-3).$   The corresponding region is a triangle, so

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(bh) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(1\cdot 1) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- The $3$rd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [-3,0).$   The corresponding region is a rectangle, so

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{3} & =bh \\  & =3\cdot 2 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

- The $4$th integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [0,5].$   The corresponding region is a trapezoid, so

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{4} & =\frac{1}{2}(a+b)h \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(3+1)(5) \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-6}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x & =-{A}_{1}+{A}_{2}+{A}_{3}+{A}_{4} \\  & =-2+\frac{1}{2}+6+10 \\  & =\frac{29}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

If the graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown above, then

${\int }_{-4}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x=$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We divide the interval of integration into $3$ regions: the arc of the semi-circle for $x\in [-4,0],$ the line segment for $x\in [0,4),$ and the line segment for $x\in (4,6].$ Using the additive property of integrals, we write

$$
{\int }_{-4}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x={{{\int }_{-4}^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{-{A}_{1}}+{{{\int }_{0}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{2}}+{{{\int }_{4}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{3}}.
$$

- The $1$st integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [-4,0].$ The corresponding region is a lower semi-circle of radius $2$, so

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}\pi {r}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\pi (2)^{2} \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Since the region lies below the $x$-axis, we have

$$
{\int }_{-4}^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{A}_{1}=-2\pi .
$$

- The $2$nd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [0,4).$ The corresponding region is a right triangle, so

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =\frac{1}{2}bh \\  & =\frac{1}{2}4\cdot 4 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

- The $3$rd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in (4,6].$ The corresponding region is a trapezoid, so

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{3} & =\frac{1}{2}(a+b)h \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4+2)\cdot 2 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-4}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x & =-{A}_{1}+{A}_{2}+{A}_{3} \\  & =-2\pi +8+6 \\  & =14-2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$
